messages.body_plain:
Here is an approach I use to check this error.  It probably isn't the most
efficient way to do it, but it works for me.  I copy the row of individual
names, (click on the first cell, then hit control-shift-right arrow, then
hit control-c), go to a new sheet, use paste special and transpose it
(bottom right option in the dialogue box that opens).  Then, highlight
that column, go to insert, then choose pivot table (left option on the
ribbon).  Select the first column name (by clicking the box beside it),
then also drag the highlighted column name down to the lower right option,
sum values.  This counts the number of times each value is present.  Copy
and paste both columns of data from the pivot table to their own columns,
then sort or filter them to find if you have any values > 1.  Those are
the duplicate names that must be changed before you can read in your data.

I'm sure Arthur has a far more efficient way of doing this though. :-)

Cheers
Peter Unmack

Hi Rafeal,

I guess I found the "problem". Your are from a country where the default in excel as a separator is a ; (colon) and not a , (comma).

This breaks the function. A simple way is either switch to English in your windows setting, or maybe easier, search replace ; with , after you saved you csv from excel.

e.g. using notepad (I assume you do not use the colon anywhere else in your names.

At least in the three lines you sent I see the colon.

*;*;*;*;*;*;*;*;*;*;*;

If you do not like this you could copy the gl.read.dart function and replace read.csv commands with read.csv2 (which has the colon as default).

Cheers, Bernd

Ps. Same in the german default setting.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Julio,

I do not think there is such a thing as a dumb question. And in any case, your question is far from easy to answer.

As I understand it, you have three individuals samples for 30 varieties. You wish to be able to assign unknown individuals to one of three categories?

(a) Variety 1 (k=1 'populations')
(b)  Variety 2 (k=1)
(c) Remainder (k=28)

I guess it would be easier if you were asking

(a)  Variety 1 or 2 (k=2)
(b) Remainder (k=28)

The challenge you face is that with only n=3 replicates for each variety, you will have substantial sampling error to deal with. So any private alleles you see in your sample may be private for the varieties, or private because of sampling error. Similar considerations will plague fixed differences or comparisons of allele frequency profiles.

The step that you have already taken, is,

gl <- gl.reassign.pop(gl, old=c(list the 28 pops here in quotes), new='remainder')
gl.report.pa <http://gl.report.pa>(gl)

Because of the sampling error issue (n=3), I think that you should consider only private alleles that are present in  Varieties 1 and 2, and not private alleles present in 'remainder'. The latter may be private alleles present in remainder (arising from 28 instances of n=3) but absent in  Variety 1 or  Variety 2 because of sampling error (one instance of n=3 in each case).

If you had a good handle of allele frequency profiles, say n=30 for each variety, then the sampling error issue would be less of a challenge and you could use assignment tests, fixed difference analysis, or filter on minor allele frequency before identifying private alleles.

Another more visual approach you might try is to do a Principal Coordinates Analysis,

pco <- gl.pcoa(gl)

and plot the results

gl.pcoa.plot(pco, gl)

to see if you get good separation of  Variety 1,  Variety 2 and remainder.

If  Variety 1 and remainder have good separation on PCoA1 (and good value for variance explained), then you can look at the factor loadings in the pco object. These are the alignments (correlations) between the original attributes (loci) and the PCoA axes. Those SNP loci that load high (have a high correlation) with Axis 1 are the ones contributing most to the separation of  Variety 1 from remainder. The private alleles should be among them, but this correlative approach is not an all or nothing thing. In combination, these high loading SNP loci should give a good indication of  Variety membership (visually if you plot the unknowns with the knowns).

There are more targetted ways of doing this (discriminant analysis) but we have not implemented them in dartR yet. You might find them elsewhere.

Also, I may not be much in advance of you in knowledge of this topic, so please take the above as suggestions only, and seek more experienced advice.

All the best,

A

Hi dartR group,

Does anyone know if the dartR package has functionality to produce Manhattan plot of allele frequencies between treatment groups? Specifically, I would like to produce a plot where the y axis = -log10 (p-values) and the x-axis = Linkage group in cM).

I have been following the GWAS tutorial by Jombart for the "adegenet" package (practicial-GWAS_day4.pdf), which dartR uses as wrappers for some of its functionality.

Jombart has examples on how to produce Manhattan plots using Fisher tests on non-genlight objects (see below), but I have been unable to find anything for genlight objects or with DArT data + rrBLUP.

Any tips appreciated!!

cheers,
Kate
